title: Akshaye Khanna Is Going Telugu — and His Villain in 'Mahakali' Could Rewrite How Bollywood Stars Cross the Border
excerpt: The Bollywood veteran joins the Prasanth Varma Cinematic Universe as demon guru Shukracharya, marking a quiet power shift in how Hindi-language actors approach South Indian cinema.
body:
In the unwritten hierarchy of Indian cinema, there has always been a certain direction to crossover traffic. South Indian stars — from Rajinikanth to Prabhas to Ram Charan — travel north to conquer Bollywood. The reverse trip, a Hindi-language star heading south with genuine creative intent rather than a dubbed voiceover, has been rarer and often awkward. Akshaye Khanna's decision to play the demon guru Shukracharya in Prasanth Varma's 'Mahakali' is interesting precisely because it doesn't feel like tourism.

Khanna, 51, is nobody's idea of a desperate career move. The son of Vinod Khanna, he spent two decades building a reputation as one of Bollywood's most reliably intelligent actors — the kind of performer who elevates middling scripts and disappears into good ones. His recent turn in 'Dhurandhar,' a sleeper hit that earned critical praise and decent box-office returns, proved he could still open a film. He doesn't need Telugu cinema. Which is exactly why his choice to enter it matters.

The Universe He's Joining

The Prasanth Varma Cinematic Universe — or PVCU — is one of the most ambitious experiments in Indian popular cinema. It began with 'Hanu-Man' (2024), a Telugu superhero origin story that earned over ₹300 crore worldwide on a relatively modest budget, proving that Indian audiences would embrace homegrown mythology-based superhero films if someone bothered to make them well. Unlike the Marvel model it superficially resembles, the PVCU draws exclusively from Hindu cosmology: its heroes are avatars, its villains are asuras, and its visual grammar owes more to temple sculpture than to comic books.

'Mahakali,' the third PVCU film, is directed by Puja Aparna Kolluru — notably, a woman at the helm of an Indian superhero franchise, a rarity that the production has been quietly highlighting. The film centres on the goddess Mahakali and expands the cosmic mythology established in 'Hanu-Man,' introducing larger-than-life antagonists and multi-realm conflicts. Shukracharya — the guru of the asuras in Hindu mythology, a figure of immense knowledge corrupted by allegiance to darkness — is exactly the kind of villain who requires an actor with gravitas, not just physicality.

The Ensemble Taking Shape

Khanna isn't the only cross-regional casting choice. Rohit Saraf, the Mumbai-based actor best known for 'Mismatched' and 'The Sky Is Pink,' recently wrapped his portion of the Hyderabad schedule, making Mahakali his Telugu debut as well. Bhoomi Shetty, a Kannada actress, anchors the cast with a role that's being kept deliberately under wraps. The multilingual casting — Hindi, Telugu, Kannada talent working under a Telugu-language production banner — mirrors the PVCU's ambition to be a truly pan-Indian franchise rather than a regional one with subtitles.

Principal photography has progressed through Kolkata and Hyderabad, with a release window of 2026-2027. The film will release simultaneously in Telugu, Hindi, Tamil, Kannada, and Malayalam.

Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

The PVCU's significance for the Indian diaspora is layered. On a surface level, it offers the kind of spectacle that NRI audiences have been buying tickets for in droves — superhero action, mythological grandeur, and the emotional weight of stories rooted in cultural identity. But there's something deeper: the PVCU is building an Indian cinematic mythology that competes with Western superhero franchises on its own terms, not as imitation but as alternative.

For diaspora families raising children between two cultures, a film universe where Hanuman and Mahakali are the heroes — not supporting characters in someone else's mythology — carries real cultural weight. It's the kind of storytelling that lets second-generation NRIs engage with their heritage through a medium they already love.

What's Next

With Akshaye Khanna's involvement confirmed and principal photography advancing, 'Mahakali' is shaping up as the PVCU's most ambitious chapter yet. Whether Khanna's crossover inspires a broader wave of Bollywood-to-Tollywood talent migration remains to be seen, but the direction of travel is clear: the creative gravity in Indian cinema is shifting southward, and smart actors are following it.
